channel.title: Nicotine Science and Policy
channel.description: Daily digest of views, debates and discussions on nicotine science, policy, regulation and advocacy.

item.title: Summer Reading: Tobacco Harm Reduction
item.description: A summer reading list on tobacco harm reduction is a reminder that this debate is built from evidence across policy, behaviour, economics and lived experience. The case for safer nicotine alternatives does not rest on one study or one country; it grows from a wider pattern showing that smokers need practical routes away from combustion. Reading across that evidence matters because prohibition, misinformation and one-size-fits-all regulation keep returning in different forms. Better tobacco policy starts with understanding the full picture, not only the arguments that fit existing assumptions. (Published on September 01, 2026byprotectingtaxpayers.org)

item.title: The FDA Is Making It Harder to Quit Smoking
item.description: A regulator can make quitting harder even while claiming to protect public health. Delayed approvals, narrow authorisation pathways and hostility towards safer nicotine products can leave adult smokers with fewer legal options than they need. Cigarettes remain widely available while alternatives that may help people switch face barriers that slow or block access. The FDA’s approach should be judged by whether it reduces smoking-related harm, not by how cautious it appears on paper. (Published on September 01, 2026byrealclearhealth.com)

item.title: Lost in the cloud: How vaping was undermined by a moral panic
item.description: Vaping was not undermined by evidence alone, but by the story built around it. Moral panic, media pressure and political caution turned a lower-risk alternative for smokers into a cultural threat that became easier to condemn than to understand. That distortion matters because fear can stop people from recognising the difference between smoke and vapour. Public health should resist panic long enough to keep the risk hierarchy clear. (Published on September 01, 2026bysubstack.com)

item.title: Changing nicotine preferences in a stable market
item.description: Changing nicotine preferences do not necessarily indicate a shrinking nicotine market. They can mean a shift in how people consume nicotine: away from cigarettes and towards pouches, snus, vaping or heated tobacco. That distinction matters because public health outcomes depend on the form of use, not only the presence of nicotine itself. A stable market can still become less harmful when policy helps consumers move away from combustion. (Published on September 01, 2026bytidsskriftet.no)

item.title: Two Countries, the Same Evidence, and Two Very Different Ideas About Helping Smokers Quit
item.description: The same evidence can lead two countries in opposite directions. One government may see safer nicotine products as part of the route away from smoking, while another treats them as a problem to restrict alongside cigarettes. That difference is not scientific; it is political. Public health policy should be judged by what it enables smokers to do in practice, not by how tightly it defends old assumptions. (Published on September 01, 2026bysubstack.com)
